Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. ## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.

- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.

- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, describe the folders the change touched in the conversation, in a text box** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Show non-test folders only, and ignore README files and comment-only changes.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

13	re-measured elsewhere, not copied.
14	
15	The one thing to keep in mind everywhere below: **speech failures are silent**. Nothing throws,
16	nothing logs, the UI keeps showing a live session — the user just hears nothing, or is heard by
17	nobody. Design each of these surfaces so every path produces exactly one observable outcome.
18	
19	## Where each API can run
20	
21	- `chrome.tts` is **not exposed to content scripts**. The session lives in the page (speech
22	  recognition needs a document, and the mic grant belongs to nytimes.com), so speaking is a
23	  relay: the content script sends `cc:speak` over the long-lived `cc-session` port and the
24	  service worker calls `chrome.tts` — `speech/remote-tts-port.js` presents the same contract as
25	  `speech/tts-port.js` so the orchestrator can't tell the difference. Prefer `chrome.tts` over
26	  `speechSynthesis` because it is immune to the page's autoplay rules (decision D2).
27	
28	## Self-echo is an application problem, not a constraints problem
29	
30	`webkitSpeechRecognition` **owns its own capture and exposes no hook for
31	`MediaTrackConstraints`** — you cannot ask the recognizer for echo cancellation. Chrome applies
32	its default AEC (a loopback of playout audio) to that capture, which already attenuates
33	`speechSynthesis`, but it misses `chrome.tts`'s OS-rendered output. So the residual echo is
34	handled at the app level by a string-match echo guard (REQ-SPCH-005), and that is the design,
35	not a stopgap (decision D11).
36	
37	Two traps around this:
38	
39	- `suppressLocalAudioPlayback` and `restrictOwnAudio` read like the fix for this and are not:
40	  they are **`getDisplayMedia` screen-capture** constraints, filtering a captured tab's own
41	  playout out of that tab's track, and `getUserMedia` ignores them without a word. The cost of
42	  reaching for one is not the dead property — it is that the echo guard that would have worked
43	  never gets written. (Enforced by the `mic-constraints-not-screen-capture` check.)
44	- The constraints you *can* set (`echoCancellation`, `noiseSuppression`, `autoGainControl`)
45	  apply only to the one capture you own — the permission preflight.
46

48

50	effect of the first listen cycle. Two rules for that preflight:
51

53	  AEC engagement only known, on the very first grant.
54	- **Retry once bare when the constrained call rejects.** A rejection is either a real denial or
55	  a browser balking at the constraint shape; only a second failure is a genuine denial. Reading
56	  a constraint quirk as "mic denied" ends the session for no reason.
57

63	keep arriving and no final result ever lands. Left alone the user repeats themselves and you get

4	watching it change, and putting your own UI into its chrome. The mechanical rules — that a
5	page observer is disconnected, that a synthetic input event bubbles — are this pack's two
6	checks; what follows is only what no check can decide for you.
7	
8	Each rule below is a judgment about being a guest in someone else's page, and holds for any
9	code that does it — a userscript, an automation layer, an extension's content script. Where
10	one cites this repo — a file, a requirement id, a date — that is the **evidence** it was drawn
11	from, not the scope it applies to.
12	
13	The premise underneath all of it: **the host will change its markup without telling you, and
14	your code will not throw when it does.** A selector that matches nothing returns null; a click
15	on a renamed button never happens. Every rule here is about making that failure loud, local,
16	and cheap to fix.
17	
18	## Quarantine the host's DOM knowledge in one module
19	
20	All of it, behind an interface expressed in your own vocabulary — here `page-adapter/` returns
21	a `Snapshot` and takes `enterAnswer`, and the crossword model, the dialog policy and the
22	matcher never learn that the page exists (REQ-PAGE-011, `dev/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` §2). Two
23	things follow, and both are worth the discipline:
24	
25	- A redesign is a **one-directory** change, and the blast radius is knowable before you start.
26	- The rest of the codebase becomes testable without a browser at all — the pure layers here
27	  (`puzzle-model/`, `matching/`, `conversation/`) are pure *because* the quarantine holds.
28	
29	Inside that module, put **every selector and class string in one file**, and change values only
30	there (`page-adapter/selectors.js`). A selector inlined at its use site is the one that gets
31	missed when the host renames a class.
32	
33	Enforce the quarantine mechanically, by token: the repo's arch test fails if the host's class
34	prefix (`xwd__`) appears in code outside `page-adapter/`.
35	
36	## Identify host UI by a net, not by a selector
37	
38	A single selector is a bet that one class name survives. Cast a net instead, and make the last
39	strand semantic:
40	
41	- class nets that accept a family (`[class*="xwd__toolbar"]`), not one exact name;
42	- attribute and role hooks the host is less likely to churn (`role="cell"`, `data-testid`,
43	  `aria-label`);
44	- and a **text/shape fallback** underneath: the splash is found by class net *or* by "a visible
45	  container whose text says 'Ready to start solving' with a Play-ish button in it, whatever its
46	  classes are called" (`page-adapter/splash.js`); the pause veil is found by its copy plus
47	  visibility (`reader.js isPaused`).
48	
49	Visibility is part of identity. Hosts keep dismissed modals in the DOM, so a match that ignores
50	`display`/`visibility`/zero-size will keep reporting a splash you already cleared.
51	
52	## Write down what you verified the selectors against, and when
53	
54	The selectors file is the only place in the codebase whose truth lives on someone else's
55	server, so it carries its own provenance: the date and page it was last verified against, the
56	captured markup it was read from, and — most valuable — the **negative** findings.
57	`selectors.js` records that the state classes sit on the `<rect>` and not the `<g>`, that the
58	pencil button exposes no `aria-pressed` and no class change, that the letter/number `<text>`
59	nodes carry no distinguishing classes and the class-based selectors match nothing live. Each of
60	those is an hour of somebody's life, and none of it is recoverable from the code.
61	
62	## Ship a probe, and make a broken page a finding rather than an exception
63	
64	One entry point that reports the health of every selector against the live page —
65	`page-adapter/probe.js`, REQ-PAGE-009, run from the in-page menu (MT-01). It is the first thing
66	to run when a user says "it stopped working", and it turns "the extension is broken" into "the
67	clue-list wrapper selector matches 0, want 2".
68	
69	It must **never throw**: a probe that dies on the first missing element reports one fault and
70	hides the other nine. Collect a row per selector and return them all — and have it capture
71	forensics for the things you could *not* read (the probe here dumps the pencil button's
72	attributes precisely because its ON state has never been readable), so the next report arrives
73	with the evidence already in it.
74	
75	## Mirror the host in a fixture, and let the fixture define the expected shape
76	
77	A saved, simplified copy of the host page (`extension-test/fixtures/fake-nyt/`, served by
78	`npm run fixture`) mirrors the selectors exactly, and the integration tests drive that. It buys
79	two things a live page cannot: the read/write/watch cycle is testable in CI at all, and the
80	whole voice loop is rehearsable locally without a subscription (`npm run build:dev` widens the
81	matches to `localhost:8787`, MT-23).
82	
83	Its limit is the same as its virtue — **the fixture only ever shows you the markup you already
84	knew about**, so a passing suite is never evidence about the live page. Keep a manual-test
85	document for what only the real host can answer (`dev/docs/MANUAL-TESTS.md`), and treat every
86	live finding as a fixture update.
87	
88	## Never trust a write — verify by re-reading
89	
90	Address the target by position rather than relying on the host's own cursor conventions (click
91	each cell, then type one letter — immune to the host's advance-on-type and skip-filled
92	settings), then **read the DOM back and confirm what you meant is there** (REQ-PAGE-007). The
93	host may ignore untrusted events, may auto-advance differently than you assumed, may reject the
94	input silently; the re-read is the only thing that distinguishes those from success.
95	
96	Poll the re-read, don't do it synchronously after the last dispatch: the host renders
97	asynchronously (React here), so the DOM immediately after your event is the DOM *before* the
98	app processed it. And aim your events at a node **inside the app's own subtree** — the selected
99	element if it has focus, otherwise a known app node. A modern app delegates key handling near
100	its root, which is a descendant of `<body>`, so an event dispatched at `document` or `body`
101	bubbles *past* it and is never seen (`page-adapter/writer.js`).
102	
103	## A synthetic keystroke must carry the fields a real one would
104	
105	The browser fills in the deprecated `keyCode`/`which`/`charCode` on every real keystroke; on
106	a synthetic one they are plain init fields that default to 0, so
107	`new KeyboardEvent('keydown', { key: 'A' })` reaches the page as a keystroke whose keyCode is
108	0. Deprecated is not the same as unread: hosts with a long-lived key-handling layer still
109	branch on the legacy fields — this one does (verified live, MT-02) — and a 0 matches nothing,
110	so the handler runs and nothing happens, indistinguishable from "the app ignores untrusted
111	events". Mirror the real event instead: `keyCode` and `which` alongside `key`/`code`,
112	`charCode` on `keypress`, and the full keydown → keypress → keyup sequence a real keystroke
113	produces (`page-adapter/writer.js` `keyEventInit`/`typeKey`).
114	
115	Build the init in **one helper** and spread it at the single dispatch site, so fidelity is one
116	function's job. That factoring is also why this rule is prose rather than a check: the init a
117	well-factored adapter dispatches is opaque to a static scan (`{ ...init }` could carry
118	anything), so a check here could only ever police code that bypasses the helper — and the
119	mistake in that code is bypassing the helper, not the field it then forgot.
120	
121	## Put back any host state you borrowed, and degrade when you cannot read it
122	
123	Driving a host toggle means driving it back: pencil mode is set to match the write and restored
124	afterwards, so the user's own typing mode is never stolen (REQ-PAGE-012).
125	
126	You will often be unable to read the state you are toggling — the live pencil button has no
127	`aria-pressed` and no class change, so "on or off?" is genuinely unanswerable. Design for the
128	unreadable case as the **normal** one, not the error case: fall back to click parity, and let
129	the feature that depends on it degrade (the letters still land; only the pencil softening is
130	lost, REQ-ANS-019) rather than failing the operation.
131	
132	## The host has a lifecycle of its own, and its blank states are not your user's doing
133	
134	You are sharing the page with an app that has its own timers, veils and modals, and each one
135	looks like something else from inside your adapter:
136	
137	- **Idle timers.** This host auto-pauses a quiet puzzle after ~30 s of no keyboard input. A
138	  voice solver touches no keyboard, so the adapter sends a bare `Shift` keydown/keyup on every
139	  heard command — a real key event that types nothing and moves nothing (REQ-LIFE-017). Choose
140	  the nudge so it cannot mutate state, and drive it from real user activity, never from a timer
141	  of your own: when the user really has gone quiet, the host *should* pause and your session
142	  should end with it.
143	- **Veils that blank the content.** The pause veil empties the visible entries. A change watcher
144	  that diffs first and checks for the veil second will read that as the user clearing the whole
145	  grid. Check for the host's own overlay states **before** diffing, report the state once, and
146	  return (`page-adapter/watcher.js`).
147	- **Pre-content splashes.** The board may not exist for minutes while a "Ready to start
148	  solving?" modal is up. Absence of the content is not absence of the app.
149	
150	## Be inert when you are off
151	
152	Your code loads on the host's page whether or not the user is using you, so **doing nothing is
153	the resting state** (REQ-NFR-004). Watchers are created on demand and stopped with the session;
154	nothing polls; nothing observes between sessions.
155	
156	Keep load-time page changes to an explicit, minimal carve-out — here exactly one: mounting the
157	toolbar button (REQ-LIFE-012). Mount it by waiting with a `MutationObserver` that **disconnects
158	the moment the element lands** (the `page-observers-disconnected` check), and give up only when
159	the host shows no app markup at all — a slow render or a splash must not cost you the button,
160	but an archive page must not leave you waiting forever.

each cell, then type one letter — immune to the host's advance-on-type and skip-filled
settings), then **read the DOM back and confirm what you meant is there** (REQ-PAGE-007). The
host may ignore untrusted events, may auto-advance differently than you assumed, may reject the
input silently; the re-read is the only thing that distinguishes those from success.

Poll the re-read, don't do it synchronously after the last dispatch: the host renders
asynchronously (React here), so the DOM immediately after your event is the DOM *before* the
app processed it. And aim your events at a node **inside the app's own subtree** — the selected
element if it has focus, otherwise a known app node. A modern app delegates key handling near
its root, which is a descendant of `<body>`, so an event dispatched at `document` or `body`
bubbles *past* it and is never seen (`page-adapter/writer.js`).

## A synthetic keystroke must carry the fields a real one would

The browser fills in the deprecated `keyCode`/`which`/`charCode` on every real keystroke; on
a synthetic one they are plain init fields that default to 0, so
`new KeyboardEvent('keydown', { key: 'A' })` reaches the page as a keystroke whose keyCode is
0. Deprecated is not the same as unread: hosts with a long-lived key-handling layer still
branch on the legacy fields — this one does (verified live, MT-02) — and a 0 matches nothing,
so the handler runs and nothing happens, indistinguishable from "the app ignores untrusted
events". Mirror the real event instead: `keyCode` and `which` alongside `key`/`code`,
`charCode` on `keypress`, and the full keydown → keypress → keyup sequence a real keystroke
produces (`page-adapter/writer.js` `keyEventInit`/`typeKey`).

Build the init in **one helper** and spread it at the single dispatch site, so fidelity is one
function's job. That factoring is also why this rule is prose rather than a check: the init a
well-factored adapter dispatches is opaque to a static scan (`{ ...init }` could carry
anything), so a check here could only ever police code that bypasses the helper — and the
mistake in that code is bypassing the helper, not the field it then forgot.

## Put back any host state you borrowed, and degrade when you cannot read it

Driving a host toggle means driving it back: pencil mode is set to match the write and restored
afterwards, so the user's own typing mode is never stolen (REQ-PAGE-012).

You will often be unable to read the state you are toggling — the live pencil button has no
`aria-pressed` and no class change, so "on or off?" is genuinely unanswerable. Design for the
unreadable case as the **normal** one, not the error case: fall back to click parity, and let
the feature that depends on it degrade (the letters still land; only the pencil softening is
lost, REQ-ANS-019) rather than failing the operation.

## The host has a lifecycle of its own, and its blank states are not your user's doing

You are sharing the page with an app that has its own timers, veils and modals, and each one
looks like something else from inside your adapter:

- **Idle timers.** This host auto-pauses a quiet puzzle after ~30 s of no keyboard input. A
  voice solver touches no keyboard, so the adapter sends a bare `Shift` keydown/keyup on every
  heard command — a real key event that types nothing and moves nothing (REQ-LIFE-017). Choose
  the nudge so it cannot mutate state, and drive it from real user activity, never from a timer
  of your own: when the user really has gone quiet, the host *should* pause and your session
  should end with it.
- **Veils that blank the content.** The pause veil empties the visible entries. A change watcher
  that diffs first and checks for the veil second will read that as the user clearing the whole
  grid. Check for the host's own overlay states **before** diffing, report the state once, and
  return (`page-adapter/watcher.js`).
- **Pre-content splashes.** The board may not exist for minutes while a "Ready to start
  solving?" modal is up. Absence of the content is not absence of the app.

## Be inert when you are off

Your code loads on the host's page whether or not the user is using you, so **doing nothing is
the resting state** (REQ-NFR-004). Watchers are created on demand and stopped with the session;
nothing polls; nothing observes between sessions.

Keep load-time page changes to an explicit, minimal carve-out — here exactly one: mounting the
toolbar button (REQ-LIFE-012). Mount it by waiting with a `MutationObserver` that **disconnects
the moment the element lands** (the `page-observers-disconnected` check), and give up only when
the host shows no app markup at all — a slow render or a splash must not cost you the button,
but an archive page must not leave you waiting forever.

# Claude Code agent proxy

Outbound HTTPS from this session goes through a local proxy at [REDACTED:env:https_proxy]
(set via HTTPS_PROXY) which tunnels to a policy-enforcing egress proxy. TLS is
re-terminated there, so every tool must trust the CA bundle at
[REDACTED:env:NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS]. The standard CA environment variables, the system trust
store (where possible), a JVM truststore, the Bazel system bazelrc, the
browser NSS store, and gsutil's boto config are already set up.

## Quick diagnosis

1. Run: curl -sS [REDACTED:env:https_proxy]/__agentproxy/status
   It reports proxy state, which trust and git accommodations are active
   (javaTrustStorePath, toolTrustFailureCodes, gitSshRewrite,
   gitConfigConflicts), and the most recent proxy-side failures.
2. Find the failure class below and apply the matching fix; gitConfigConflicts
   codes map to the git section, toolTrustFailureCodes to the JVM section.
3. Never disable TLS verification, never unset HTTPS_PROXY, and do not retry
   organization policy denials (403/407) — report them instead.

## Failure classes and fixes

### "certificate verify failed" / "self-signed certificate in chain" / PKIX errors

The failing tool is not reading the pre-set CA configuration. In order:
